paragraphs: Haha)) Remember about six months ago we were reasoning here that everything is heading toward us simply telling the model what we want to happen, and it becoming its problem how to do it?
I hope everyone has already appreciated the fresh /goal <objective> in the new CLI release?;)
Not in the Codex APP yet, but that's …, it's already in the CLI )))))
This is no soup of seven LOOPs.
You simply make a plan, or just say what you want to exist, after /goal, and the model won't stop until you get it.
But I'd still do it through a plan, because otherwise at some point it may drag the result in by the ears:)
Stuck a huge plan into /goal before bed; curious what I'll see tomorrow morning:)
I've been thinking about this for only a short while, but the longer I think, the more the hair stirs on my head) EXCITED
I have a huge development, and as we know — huge development = HUGE PROBLEMS =)
They're of course far from always huge, but there are … of them.

And the joke is that some of these problems have such a nasty little character. To the ear they sound downright funny, elementary. In practice they don't get solved on the third, or the fifth, or the eighteenth attempt.

Sooner or later they do get solved, because a problem like “anchors on Microsoft drop off the SMTP engine faster than we manage to send an email from them” is a problem I can't not solve, since it's sort of one of the foundations of the system I'm building.
Solving that puzzle took me more than ten hours, which means no fewer than ten prompts. Actually I think even more than 20.

Even if we assume they were lazy “think again” ping-prompts — that's still 20 such prompts. They demanded my attention 20 times. 20 times caused frustration at the failure resulting from the prompt's work. 20 times this, 20 times that. Brought me a full twenty steps closer to believing in God, a.k.a. exiting current reality into an imaginary one where the evil … spirits won't touch me, and I could humbly live out my miserable life in poverty with one armor-piercing answer to everything.
And that's not the only task like that.
And then… /goal

I can tell this … once what I need and what I consider the result in the given matter. For the problem described above you don't even need a long prompt — I briskly listed just 10 parameters and two emotional lines, the fingers won't get tired.
That's how much frustration off the shoulders per week? That's how many times you don't have to send a prompt with a crooked …?

Honestly — this is the main innovation of the quarter, in my view, comparable to 5.5 itself, I think even exceeding it in significance, since the previous models already coded fine; everything I have working was written before 5.5 =)
C'EST LA VIE …!!!!!!!!!
We'll break through, finish it off, we don't lose!!!
On one hand these 2+ million lines were written more easily than ever by anyone in history, by the nature of what's happening.
On the other hand, in blood) My brain has already … told me off so many times over these couple of months… Sometimes it even gives me chills, like a fever, toward five in the morning.

But … all the LLMs already agree that we've implemented about 80% of the vision. What's left is the simplest in terms of code and the hardest in terms of design. The brain crunches, the bastard, but it's not going anywhere)
Funny that some things I … over my shoulder to myself while writing down the vision end up requiring simply unreal effort.

How about this task: think through a multilayered AI research machine which, regardless of product type, can give birth to hundreds of hypotheses, then, having automatically collected human feedback, adjust their weighting, and test them with hundreds of types of … logical emails?

Sounds nice, of course. But you still have to … build it. And when you start designing this …, there's … no bottom in sight at all. And all of it has to be held in mind, written down, rewritten; I'm … writing prompts now far longer than any longreads I ever wrote. And how many of those have there been? Several a day; I … how many thousands of pages have been filled to end up at the current point.
Truly, vibe-coding is no simpler than writing books. Honestly, writing books now seems like a very simple task =)

The difference is that a book you can simply not write, whereas not finishing vibe-coding the thing you've … so many months into, and bet so much on, and know how it'll help rake in the dough — that you CAN'T =))))))))))
For those who'll latch on now, like, … yourself, why are you in Claude, where's your beloved Codex.
In short, Claude performs two functions for me now:

1) It's very useful from time to time to ask Claude, speaking with my mouth into the watch, to look at Codex's last 10 commits and search the derivatives of those commits for bugs/glitches/room for optimization. Without distracting Codex from creation, so to speak.
2) When all 4 Codex Pro subscriptions are exhausted, about 1.5–2 days remain, and those 1.5–2 days I finish off on the Claude subscription)
The nearest Codex dries up at 6:37 a.m. San Francisco time tomorrow, and I'll be grinding on Codex again until the 4 subscriptions … over the next 4.5 days =)
That's how we live. At the moment.
There's no point planning how we live in principle right now; every 2 weeks we live some new way ))))))

Honestly — this is the main innovation of the quarter, in my view, comparable to 5.5 itself, I think even exceeding it in significance, since the previous models already coded fine; everything I have working was written before 5.5 =)
Yesterday I set /goal for the night, so I could marvel at exciting novelties in the morning.
It turned out that our entire ambitious plan was implemented through Goal and tested e2e in… 1h 10m.
The plan consisted of 16 tasks and an open invitation to add subtasks if it ran into a problem that couldn't be calculated in advance.
Usually such a plan on 5.5 xhigh took the model 12–20 hours.
I was thinking it was probably done …, and now I'd have to redo it the old-fashioned way.
But no, everything actually works as intended.
I went to look at the /goal run history and understood what the trick is.
/goal is, in short, an innovation on the level of the release of Codex itself.
It's just that big things in space sometimes have a whimsical shape; sometimes they're even hard to see.
In the /goal run history I saw the following:

1) A pittance of extra output compared to a typical request. The model in /goal is a model “in focus.” It basically doesn't … care what's happening around it; it … toward the goal at some otherworldly speed, knowing there are no limits.

Funny, but the model in principle hurries to finish its work faster in order to save resources; that's the basis of its existence. That's where our problem lived. The operator's job is a game of prompts against the model's habit of finishing work as fast as possible. The more an operator can squeeze out of the model in 1 run, the more they'll squeeze out of it over dozens of runs.
That way the operator saves their own energy and overtakes the other Runners.
And now the model simultaneously hurries to finish faster, but…. can't, until the conditions of <objective> are met.
It's like a dog with a sausage tied to a stick, always dangling in front of its nose.
2) Absence of ritual pulsation.

When you address the model, it has a specific structure of actions: read these docs, go into those folders, scratch its butt, sketch a plan of a plan of a plan, refine the plan of the plan, choose a plan, scratch its belly, just in case go recheck all the repos, the whole computer, the whole server over SSH, think a little, then the work begins, which at some point ends, and the exit ritual begins: dessert, digestif, napkins, wash hands, leave the restaurant a review, share the review with all friends, etc.

Coding this way is infinitely faster and more reliable than …, but compared to the /goal mechanics, it's like flying halfway around the planet with layovers in EVERY CITY along the route — barely took off and already landing — vs. taking off once and flying straight through.

Besides the time spent, I saved some simply unintelligible number of tokens. Usually when I wake up in the morning, having set a loop before bed on a budget close to 100%, I'm used to seeing 50–60% remaining on the counter, which I then … down by six in the evening of the new day with three sessions on top of the continuing loop, and hop to the next subscription.
Today I woke up and the counter shows 88%, even though in parallel with /goal I launched a very … task which, judging by the time of the last commit, ran 4 times longer than /goal itself.
So /goal devoured barely 3–4% of the weekly quota, whereas usually this task ate 40–50%. So it got 12+ times …:))

I made a most detailed plan-ledger in which the overall development is broken into a heap of subtasks, plus stretching Claude Code's design onto it on the fly during development, and asked Codex to help me formulate the correct request for /goal so that all of it would be developed and tested as the outcome of the /goal run
Codex gave me the correct request, I stuck it in and went to sleep)

Very many things that are AI-demanding in my system I've given up implementing via API, and gone the route of webhook-triggering a Codex session to implement them. This makes especially much sense for one-off big tasks.

You can of course pile up 15 requests to 3 different models for cost-efficiency, which then get checked by another 10 requests for quality control and refinements, but even if you do 100 passes — it's less reliable than simply triggering Codex with the right context passed into it and a prompt baked into a button or trigger, and waiting for Codex to do its thing. And the longer you play with this approach, the more cool interface solutions you come up with that turn the interface into literal magic) Through AI tokens it's …, unreliable, expensive. Whereas here you're already paying for 4 Codex subscriptions anyway, and the computer is always on.

If some automation works really well and you're afraid the computer won't be on — well, …, you can buy a Raspberry Pi 5, plug it into the router, and know that one $200 session exists solely to serve these processes. I have a hard time imagining (so far) a set of processes in one project capable of burning the entire weekly limit of a $200 Codex subscription. Let's talk about it in a month:)))))

BUT THE SPECIAL PLEASURE comes from jamming in terminal-like interfaces with filling progress that Codex very gallantly marks as it works (since we explicitly ask it to in the prompt baked into the button, lol).
It feels like I'm in a movie about the future — distant, crappy, real, Ridley Scott-esque =)

You just press a button — and an animation beautifully unfolds a terminal and indicators beneath it. Reasoning starts running across the terminal, and the indicators fill up, get marked with green checkmarks, light up with yellow or red anxious alerts if something's wrong, and all of this happens right in your interface. Never before has the WEB been so cinematically crossbred with game interfaces. Only in game interfaces it was practically a GIF — linear as …. Whereas on the web, with current AI capabilities, it's literally the antonym of a GIF. Antonym, by the way, is a … word. They won't call just any … an ANTONym (sounds of furious self-congratulation):*

It's especially pleasant to realize that any NON-GREEN alert, hinting that something isn't perfect, launches a neighboring session that fixes the cause, while the current session continues, KNOWING thanks to prompting that a bad alert isn't a blocker, it'll soon be fixed, and the rest can be done in the meantime.

These sessions can even be taught to communicate with each other through a file… And then the mother session can learn to check whether the rescuer session has crashed or was born dead, and revive it if it … isn't emitting reasoning into the file…
How beautiful this is, Lord, create some more … like this, I really like it!!!
